utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, the 8th of June, 2009. I would like to greet Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak also, who's testifying, as well as all Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer and his associates, without forgetting all the people assisting us in this courtroom. I will first and foremost give the floor to our Registrar, who has an IC number to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The fourth batch of 3D list of documents tendered via Witness Slobodan Praljak shall be given Exhibit IC1025. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. As you know, Mr. Praljak's testimony will come to an end. Since he has presented or will finish presenting all his arguments and documents, I would like to specify that you may have noticed that when I put a question, the question is rather a lengthy one. Why do I put rather lengthy questions? Well, this is because, as an unbiased Judge, I should not demonstrate any bias whatsoever. Therefore, before I put a question, I make quite sure that I put a question against the backdrop of a more general context, I refer to the document already quoted, and I refer to the words of the witness or to what other witnesses have said, because I wish to be as neutral as possible. This is why my questions are very long. The witness before us must understand that the Judge before him is impartial, that we are there to get to the truth. This is what I wanted to tell you, Mr. Praljak, because you must have been a little bit surprised, you, like others, by my rather lengthy questions. This is because I wish to demonstrate my total impartiality, and this is why my questions are sometimes rather long. That said, I shall now give the floor to Ms. Pinter, who will resume her examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The legal officer has just reminded me that I have an oral decision to hand down. I had forgotten about it because I was concerned about the length of my questions. So this escaped me. This is a very short oral decision. Oral decision relating to the response time of the motion filed by the Prlic Defence to reopen the proceedings. On the 2nd of June, 2009, the Prlic Defence filed a motion asking for the case to be reopened in order to hear the expert witness Schindler. On the 4th of June, 2009, the Praljak Defence supported the Prlic Defence's motion. The Trial Chamber would like to draw the attention of the parties of the response time they have to respond to this motion. As far as the reopening of the proceedings is concerned, the Trial Chamber expects these responses to come in 14 days after the filing of the Prlic Defence, i.e., on the 16th of June, 2009. The Trial Chamber would like to recall and [indiscernible] everyone that in this particular case Rule 94 bis (B) cannot be applied. This Rule stems from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber would also like to remind all the parties who wish to respond that at this juncture their submissions have nothing to do with the type of witness, but can only relate to the reopening of the proceedings as filed by the Prlic Defence. So you have until the 16th of June, 2009, at the latest, to submit your submissions on the reopening of the proceedings as filed by the Prlic Defence. That said, Ms. Pinter, you now have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear the English? Is everything working?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Would you turn to document P00524 first, please, and we're still dealing with the binder titled "Documents to Explain." And it is the minutes from the Presidential Office of the 26th of September, president of the Republic of Croatia, that is. Did you attend that meeting? You did attend that meeting, and we see the agenda on page 1. What can you tell us about the topics discussed and the agenda? And what can you tell us about the problems that you had with HOS in the Republic of Croatia as well, because we already heard about that in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend that meeting. And in view of the time we have left, I'll go through point 1 quickly, because point 1 is important, where Dr. Franjo Tudjman is talking about the addendum to the agreement on cooperation with the BiH, and he summarises all the problems there. He's referring to the appendix of the agreement on cooperation and friendship with the BiH, and he says that Izetbegovic, at a meeting of the UN, asked for a meeting with Dr. Tudjman, with the proposal that they coordinate their action, military action, of course, and he even went further than that and asked that the Croatian forces be ordered -- that is to say, the HV be ordered to enable all the BH Army supplies to be furnished; and he says that this is being impeded. Of course, there wasn't enough weapons even with the HV, let alone the HVO. And then he goes on to say that if the supplies were to go through Herzegovina, that then the army would lift the blockade of Sarajevo. Dr. Tudjman responded and said that he was in favour of cooperation, speaking for Croatia, but as far as the HVO was concerned, that was a problem, first of all, with the Croatian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, first and foremost. And then he mentions that at the beginning -- that is to say, Franjo Tudjman proposed a military clause to be incorporated in the agreement between two countries and that Mr. Izetbegovic rejected that, which is also correct. Secondly, he goes on to state that Croatia does not want a long, drawn-out war, but was in favour of a political solution, and that Mr. Izetbegovic didn't want that. And then he says that he signed a draft of an agreement just to sign it for the sake of signing it, in fact, to give him the opportunity of getting his supplies from Croatia. And he goes on to say very clearly that we're all conscious of the importance of the joint interest of the two countries and the two presidents, the presidents of those two countries, and that it was to protect sovereignty, integrity, autonomy, of the two countries, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he goes on to note that the Serb forces are attacking from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on and so forth. So, in actual fact, on the following page, he once again says that diplomatic and political steps should be speeded up to find a political solution. He talks about the readiness for self-defence and joint defence on the part of the two countries, and that is why a board was set up to coordinate these actions, and I became part of that board, as was -- there was General Bobetko and so on. It says that human rights would be respected and criminals be punished. And then we come to a whole series of views and assertions to the effect that -- the question asked is what the international community wants, and Dr. Tudjman realises that the embargo will not be withdrawn and that -- lifted, and that his speech, that is to say, Izetbegovic's speech at the United Nations, was geared towards war, and that's how everybody else understood it. And there's mention again about this joint board for coordination between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, because it is understood here, too, that there are disturbing incidents and that control should be assumed in the territories liberated by the HVO; that is to say, the majority population. And he goes on to say that he doesn't agree that the question of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be solved after the war, and says that at the time he's speaking, that the internal setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina must be considered, which is something that I said, that Izetbegovic told me at the meeting in Mostar, that -- he said, Let's go and win, and then we'll reach the agreements, whereas I said that in a war, had you to agree on a setup on the internal system of Bosnia-Herzegovina so that the people who were fighting and losing lives and being killed would know what their goal was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Praljak kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Just now, the interpreter asked us, asked me to ask Mr. Praljak to slow down. It is my first request to him, addressed to him. The second one, that I missed the page which he referred to. Please kindly tell us about what pages are you talking now, if there is any particular page or pages which you would like us to have a look at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0186-2841 is the first page number, and it goes on to 842 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, not all the pages have been translated, some of the ones that you referred to. They're not all in English. That's why I wanted to interrupt you, to tell you that, and also to ask you to tell us the portions that have been translated. You don't have to read the minutes. You can tell us about them because you were there, so you know what they were about without having to read them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not really reading, but I will try and speak slower. Anyway, Mr. Izetbegovic repeats here that he does not want to say precisely what kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina he envisages and wants to see, and then he said quite openly that he already had a 50 per cent majority, and that it would be a civil state, and that they would grant rights to others. Of course, they cannot grant any rights to anybody else, because those rights belong to the Croatian people under the constitution, because they're a sovereign constituent people. Furthermore, they went on to speak about the terrible problem that the embargo was creating, fully conscious of the fact that it would not be lifted, and this is something that all international factors repeated. He said that there would be no military intervention. And throughout, during the whole meeting, in actual fact, two states are talked about and their internal system, the internal system and setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the desire of Croatia that the -- the fervent desire of Croatia to help and to assist, but not to prolong the war, but to try to find a peaceful solution. So that is the gist of what was discussed at the meeting and what I can tell you. I can't give you the page numbers, but it's a long text, and I think it is one of the more important minutes which speak for itself. It's crystal clear, defining the political position of the entire Croatian leadership. And later on you'll see that the government and parliament and the president of the state, the security -- National Security Council and everybody else was of this same opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say for Their Honours that that portion has been translated, because we were discussing point 1 of the agenda.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And it was an appendix to the agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that portion has been translated; that is to say, point 1 of the agenda exists in English. General, you attended the meeting, and we have your portion of the discussion here, when you took the floor. Perhaps we could explain to Their Honours what you said and the reason and circumstances under which you uttered them. And that is to be found on page 01862856. 01862856 is the number, that's right, and in English it is page 17 out of 71 pages, and it goes on to page 19.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the floor for the first time here and I say something that we're all aware of, that is common knowledge, and that is that in all the information we received about the refugee centres and all their bases on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and mention was made of the fact that they were allowed to walk around freely, buying weapons on the black market and so on and so forth, it was quite improper behaviour within the confines of another state. They considered it to be their base and thought they could do whatever they liked there. So that's what I talk about, and I say that at their staffs, those staffs of theirs, they reject any possible talks about Herceg-Bosna, both in Baska Voda, in Brela and so on, where these meetings were taking place. And then I go on to say that the refugees who arrived on the territory where the Croatian people were in Bosnia-Herzegovina either in the majority, where the Croats had the majority, or almost the majority, that the picture had changed and that they should be allowed to enter Croatia and to be sent abroad. So that's what I said, that the problem should be internationalised to the maximum, because while it was only us resolving it, nobody asked whether we had enough money to do that, whether we had fuel for transport, whether we had vehicles to transport the wounded. Everybody would come into the country, but failed to see the magnitude of the problem that faced Croatia, both in material terms and military terms, and in all other aspects as well. So I say that the population settled there was a sort of ethnic occupation that had taken place when the Serbs expelled the Muslims. Unless that situation was solved politically, then it would be within a civil state and that no -- they wouldn't have the necessary rights. So that's what I'm saying, that they were talking about the green transversal, the green line towards the sea, and we're talking about 1992, and this can be seen from the discussions held from Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar, this general line moving towards the coast, and this was a topic that was bandied about publicly. They said that they were waiting for us to get tired of the Serbs and then they would come into action and take over militarily. And Mr. Izetbegovic obviously saw that the international community, even after Cutileiro's plan, were recognising the state of affairs on the ground. So if that was to succeed, nobody would worry about the rights of nations -- well, the fact that the nation was a sovereign one and constituent one, and so on and so forth. So that roughly is what this is about and what I said, and this board was set up to cooperate with Bosnia-Herzegovina; Bobetko, Praljak and Koljevic, I think, were the three members put forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. All the rest is in the exhibit, so we don't have to go through those documents. But look at P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'd like to get back to the beginning of this document, the very beginning of it. This is a meeting which you attend. You're one of the few survivors still present, since a number of participants have died, so you witnessed this meeting which took place on the 26th of September, 1992. Something drew my attention, and this was the intervention of Mr. President Tudjman, who says, for the United Nations, that the president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina mentioned the fact that they needed to coordinate their actions, and he says there is a problem with the HVO, and he says the first of these problems is the relationship they have with the Croatian people. My question is a lengthy one, because I need to set it against the indictment. When I read that, I think, and it states in the indictment, that the HVO is at the source of the joint criminal enterprise, and Mr. Tudjman admits that there is a problem with the HVO. You attended this meeting. What do you have to say to this? What do you have to say about what Mr. Tudjman said about the HVO? Was this criticism he levelled at the HVO or not? How did you understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, Tudjman did not create the HVO. The HVO was created as a spontaneous and later on organised, well, God knows to what extent, the need of the people to defend themselves against the aggression mounted by the Yugoslav People's Army and the Republika Srpska Army. Here, Tudjman speaks about the relationship between two states, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, but he says, Mr. Izetbegovic, first of all, you didn't sign the military agreement that I offered to you, the military agreement between two states, but just the border and so on, lest the Serbs should get offended. Secondly, secondly, we are providing weapons, Croatia is providing weapons, in spite of the embargo, and this is creating enormous problems. But, Mr. Izetbegovic, the problem is the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You have the HVO down there and the Croatian people. Explain what is the political platform for the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Make a deal with the HVO. The HVO is part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it is an expression of the will of the people, and they are defending themselves. They managed to defend themselves, because while Mr. Izetbegovic was telling tall tales about the Yugoslav People's Army as the guarantor of peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we managed to defend ourselves and the Muslims and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, Mr. Praljak is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he has nothing to do with that. And he says, Please, agree about an internal structure organisation. Yes, I'm sorry. Present us with a political platform, which Mr. Izetbegovic never did present. It was always said that there would be a civil state in all circles, Muslims had the 50 per cent majority, and they always said, You will be given rights. And, Your Honour, I don't want anyone to give me -- grant me any rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have my rights under the constitution, and nobody can grant me rights and nobody can strip me of those rights, except by force, of course. So this is the response. Franjo Tudjman had as much to do with the HVO as he had with the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at document P03821. It's the 30th of July, 1993. It's a report submitted by Goran Vucica to the Petar Kresimir the IV Brigade, and it has to do with Uskoplje, Gornji Vakuf and Prozor area. You are familiar with this document, and now I would like to ask you if you could tell us why is this document important? What should we know, apart from the fact that we have the disposition of the BH Army forces? What else should we know and what would you like to bring our attention to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to bring your attention to just a couple of things. First of all, Mr. Vucica's report is false. He is lying. Secondly, he is in charge of a small unit, a professional unit of the HVO. Thirdly, he has refused to obey his orders. And now as to why he doesn't want to obey the orders, he's just talking nonsense, saying that he received some information from me and then in Rama, so in my forward command post he received some other explanations, and only a liar could say something like that. And, thirdly, this report of his -- of course, he refused to obey an order. He took his unit and went home, and then the brigade commander receives a report from him in which he says, Well, we simply decided to do it this way and my lads agreed that I am in the right of it. So, Your Honours, this is what I have been saying about the double chain of command. Who is in command of this person? Who exercises command over him? I don't know, of course, but I couldn't exercise command over him. He simply up and went. And since it was a war and I didn't have the time, it took me one month to have him removed from this post because there was fighting throughout the month and it's impossible to deal with the problem in such circumstances, and to even just write an order and to initiate the procedure for his removal, it takes time. I, in the end, managed to do it, but this is proof that there existed another chain of command. And this was not the only example. This was just the most blatant one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm seeing this document for the first time, as are all the other people. It seems to show that in this brigade, some officers challenged your leadership. It is obvious, since it is said here that there were several of them who agreed with him, and you said that he went back home. This may show the problems you encountered exercising your leadership. However, in such a situation as this, and I'm very cautious in asking this question, was it impossible for you to arrest this man and to have him tried, without delay, before a military court for insubordination, or was it absolutely impossible for you to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely impossible, Your Honour, absolutely impossible. Given the situation, it was absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But Goran Vucica was removed from his post later on. We saw a document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, but it took a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at document P03971. It's a report by Luka Markesic, sent to the HVO Presidency and the Rama Brigade Command. The date is the 5th of August, 1993. That was the time when you were in Herceg-Bosna because you were the commander of the HVO, so what can you tell us about this document? Do you have any knowledge as to who are the higher levels or higher echelons that ordered the arrests of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no idea. I don't know anything about this document. This is the first time that I see it. It was sent to the HVO Presidency and to the command of the brigade. Why to the Presidency of the HVO and Rama? Well, it's probably the HVO Presidency in Rama, probably. I can't tell you anything more about this document, and I don't know who the higher-ups or the higher echelons are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But you were not among them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to look at document P06203. It's a document dated the 28th of October, 1993. Colonel Zeljko Siljeg is writing to the assistant head of the Defence Department, Medical Section. Are you familiar with this document and can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not familiar with this document, but I am aware of the fact that this document was drafted, because I was in contact with Siljeg, and I don't have any comments to make. Well, Siljeg states quite clearly here that what he received -- the fact that he received an order on the 28th about the people in detention centres and so on and so forth, that as far as the operational zone that he is commanding is concerned, it has nothing to do with it. He's not part of the chain of command in the Medical Sector, and as the commander of the operational zone he does not have the institutions and persons in question. And he says that the brigades are only to report to the military district commander, so he's the wrong address, both as regards the form and the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Siljeg also speaks about the jurisdiction over those centres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He says quite clearly that this is not within the jurisdiction of the operational zone, and the HVO is the military component.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to look at document P06937. It's a document dated the 8th of November, 1993. It's an order signed by Zlatan Mijo Jelic, and your signature and the stamp are also there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, General Praljak's Defence has also filed a motion regarding this document, and we were told that we should be -- that we should deal with it in the course of our Defence case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. I have a question with regard to the previous document, which refers to an order also, I think, of 28 October which apparently was not correctly drafted. Mr. Praljak, do you know what order Siljeg is speaking about or writing about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Medical Sector obviously addressed him, asking him about those detention centres where detainees were. They asked him some questions, and he tells them, Well, we don't have such centres, we don't know about any such centres, nor can you ask something like this from us. So in formal legal terms, you cannot issue an order to us because we're not part of your chain of command, and in terms of the contents of this order, we have nothing to tell you because such institutions are not under the jurisdiction of the operational zone commanders or the Main Staff indeed. So that's it, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: As regards the Main Staff, this is your addition?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I added to it, because you cannot have something in the operational zone without it being automatically under the jurisdiction of the Main Staff, so I would have known about that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do we have that order, that order of the medical side; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence was unable to find it because the reference number is not listed, and there is nothing in there which would make it possible for us to search for it in the EDS or in the archives, so we have been unable to find it. We only have this date, the 28th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, let us go back to document P06937. It's a document that has already been admitted into evidence, and we have filed motions in which we have claimed -- well, perhaps you could first tell us what you have to say about this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of November, 1993, I had a meeting in Tomislavgrad. I spent a night there. In the morning of the 8th, I was in that area, waiting for Mr. Roso, and I spent the afternoon and the evening with him because he was supposed to take over that post in the area of Livno and Tomislavgrad. In the Main Staff Command, I came after 10.30 and I signed two documents. One was to speed up the investigation regarding Stupni Do, and this document had been drafted by Mr. Petkovic, but I wanted tighter dead-lines, because Mr. Petkovic at the time, on that day, and over those days, he was in Split and he wanted to get some rest, to visit his family. And the other document is the one about, well, allowing UNPROFOR -- regarding the wounded persons in East Mostar. This is a forgery. Why was this document forged, and there's another one that was also forged? Well, I don't know; probably to bring me here before this Tribunal. And, well, on that day, I did not -- I was not there. I arrived at the Main Staff after 10.30, around 11.00. And for me to sign "General Slobodan Praljak" below "Zlatan Mijo Jelic," well, this makes no sense. Your Honours, this has nothing to do with me. This is a forgery that was created in various forges that you know had a lot to do with the work of this Tribunal. I don't want to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But let us give a territorial delineation. The 2nd Brigade of the HVO, where was it active?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you indeed indicated the list of documents of which you said they were forged. When I ask my questions, which is going to be in two weeks' time, I do intend to return at length to this document and other documents. This is why I'm not asking questions about this right now, but rest assured I have a whole lot of questions related to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer every question, Your Honour. But it is interesting to note that firing on the Old Bridge on the 8th, and all of that and documents of this sort, are created on the last day of my stay in that area. But be that as it may, I don't have evidence, but I do know that there are plots and conspiracies, and I claim -- I claim that this is not mine. I never signed anything of the sort. And for me to sign just like that, without saying "approved" or anything like that, for somebody simply to forge my signature there, I don't know. Well, in the normal documents, you would normally have "Commander of the Main Staff, General Slobodan Praljak," it's typed out, and here it's handwritten. So I really don't know. It probably was photocopied from a document and then appended to it. But I really state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I think it's better to keep this for later, because right now everything is taken from your time. So I think it's better to leave this for the time when I ask my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, we've finished with that binder. And since we're on the subject of Mostar, we can move on to discuss the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can do the snipers if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, for the Trial Chamber we have prepared the documents that we're going to deal with next. In the book, "How the Old Bridge Was Destroyed," we have a letter that we prepared for the Trial Chamber especially, which is 3D01469, and I'd like to ask the usher or Registrar to hand over these documents to the Trial Chamber. That's just the letter, but we also have prepared the book titled "How the Old Bridge Was Destroyed," which is 3D00374.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, you have the book in front of you, and you have the letter, too. But before we discuss the letter, let me say that we've already heard a lot about the Old Bridge. Do you have anything to add linked to the book or the event, the incident or whatever?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do. I claim that -- well, Judge Antonetti frequently says, You're under oath, you've taken the solemn declaration, and I state what I've already stated. I protected the Old Bridge in 1992. While I was the commander of the Main Staff, I did my best to protect it from being shot at, although it was a military target. We were all aware of that. I also claim and assert that I only learnt of the Old Bridge's destruction in Zagreb or going on my way, after I'd handed over my duties on the 9th, in the morning. I heard it over the radio, news of the Old Bridge having been destroyed, and that there was a -- as for the tank that was shooting at the bridge, I had absolutely no idea about that. I was there on the 8th, but I had completed my duties. And then, Your Honours, a whole avalanche fell upon me from the international public and the domestic public, saying that Praljak and the HVO had destroyed the Old Bridge. Now, all my attempts as a human being to state that I did not do that, that I had nothing to do with that, they all fell through, because this terrible avalanche of lies gained momentum and snowballed, we had a snowball effect, until I heard that even the president of the republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, came to believe the rumour. And in 1997, here I am writing to him. I don't use any -- I don't say, Honourable President, or anything. I just go on to say, Mr. President, and then set out the fact that I had nothing to do with the bridge's destruction. I asked to be received by him, and I suppose, obviously under this avalanche of lies, and he must have given them -- he must have thought them credible, anyway, he asked all these people -- all the people dealing with the secret services - let's call them that - to report to him and to complete the investigation into the bridge's destruction. So this is a trial and conviction beyond and outside the law, with just using pamphlets and slogans and no proper investigation. And as this situation continued, Your Honours, at my own initiative I started to investigate the matter myself, because I don't want my name to be linked in any way to that event, or the HVO, and so I went around collecting material and documents that I had access to because I saw that there was some murky -- there was some murky games afoot. I state quite certainly that neither Praljak nor the HVO had anything to do with the bridge's destruction. And then I took three of the best experts in the area of explosives, the best experts from Croatia, experts in explosives, and then I also contacted a professor from Germany, and gave them the assignment to investigate how the Old Bridge was actually destroyed. And we had witness recently who testified here. She said that she was near the Old Bridge, attending a meeting when the bridge was destroyed, and that she heard a very loud explosion, and she emphasised that, and that explosion was certainly not caused by a tank; it was caused by explosives that were planted underneath the bridge and that destroyed the bridge. And that is the conclusion that the experts have reached, so I reject having anything to do -- I deny having anything to do with the destruction of the Old Bridge. It's just been cooked up in somebody else's kitchens and pots.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record and for Their Honours, this relates to Witness BD, and (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the man who filmed the destruction, this Scotsman or English soldier who later on went to Sarajevo, got into a plane and published -- made it all public, well, Their Honours, you could ask the British government to send you a report, who the man was, how he happened to board the plane, how he happened to have been there, and what role he played in all that, and who he played that role with, and, furthermore, why nobody ever completed the investigation that had been started. Now, in whose interest that is, I don't know. That surpasses my powers of deduction and proof and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, as you mentioned the inquiry, I'd like to ask you to look at page 39 of the book, and on e-court it is page 3D16-0040. And for the English version, it is 3D16-0119. This is the request for an investigation to be undertaken into the whole incident. You mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 23rd of November, 1993, is the date. However, Ms. Nika, I, at my own initiative, wrote letters and asked the international community, which in a way had taken control of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was in control - you had judges there, an ombudsman, and high representatives and whatever - to start an investigation or, rather, to continue the investigation and to establish what had happened. But they found the culprit, and that culprit's name is Slobodan Praljak. But I say it's not Slobodan Praljak. Let me repeat that. It is not Slobodan Praljak. I don't know about the shots from the tank, but the destruction of the bridge was not caused by the HVO or Slobodan Praljak. Who destroyed it, I don't know. We'll probably learn about this in 40 or 50 years' time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Old Bridge from Hum Hill could have been destroyed with three shells in the space of one minute, had I wanted to do that. Let's make that understood. Three shells, a maximum of three shells from Hum Hill. I was the commander there from the 24th until the 8th, in the throws of the attack, when they were attacking with large-scale offensives, when soldiers were crossing the bridge and weapons being taken across the bridge, and the Old Bridge was not shot at, because I did not let -- allow anybody to shoot at the Old Bridge. And then they destroyed it at nine -- on the 9th at 10.00. I left my position, but who cares about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I have to repeat the question, because it wasn't recorded. But you don't have to repeat your answer, General. That's been recorded. And the question is this: While the general was the commander of the HVO, were there any orders to shoot at the bridge, to target the bridge.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I've explained why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, could you inform the Chamber on what kind of shell you are thinking about when you say that, "with three of them." Do you mean three shells hitting or three shells shot, and what kind of shells with what kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a 130-millimetre cannon which was up on Hum Hill, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. There are shells which have delayed fire-power. The Old Bridge is hollow, it was hollow, and if, with a shell, you move this retarded or delayed charge, then the shell hits the bridge at the point of the arch, where the arch is, penetrates it, and explodes inside. Now, most probably a bridge hit in that way would fall with just one shell. Three are quite sufficient. And you saw on the photograph how, when you're up on Hum Hill, you can see the bridge as if it were on the palm of your hand, and if during the large-scale offensive that they were launching in mid-September to the 10th of October, when the bridge -- when the Old Bridge was the main military means used to transfer their forces and MTS from Hum to West Mostar and to the right bank, if you bear that in mind, so not only did I not shoot, but I forbid anybody to shoot at the Old Bridge, even when it was quite obvious that it was a military target, and any army in the world would have destroyed it, the American Army or anybody else. So if I didn't allow anybody to shoot at the bridge then, then on the 8th, 9th, I was not there, so it was organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, was that a written order forbidding any shots being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, it was not written. Your thesis, that you hit this bridge with an artillery shell, what is -- thinking of ballistics, what is -- how many shots do you have to fire to be sure that you fire -- that you actually hit a target of that size? Did you calculate that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, up on that hill, if you take the photograph on page -- if you look at the photograph on page -- well, you can see it. You can use a barrel. You have an artillery shot, a straight one. You don't have to have an elevation. You can't miss it from that distance, with that kind of visibility. You cannot miss, you couldn't miss the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, maybe we would need an artillery expert to say how much the dispersion is, because there's always a dispersion, as you very well know as well as I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'm going to try and save time, because this issue of the Old Bridge has been discussed for hours on end, whilst - and I'm saying this to everybody - there's not even one sentence on the destruction of the Old Bridge in the pre-trial brief, although the bridge is something extremely relevant for all the communities in Mostar. Let me tackle the issue from a different angle, in the most legal and scientific manner possible. There was a tank, and we know that there were three soldiers in the tank, Tomo Topic, Dragan Rezic and Senaid Cavcic. These three soldiers were heard by the SIS. They made statements. Unfortunately, we -- I do not have their statements right now, but - and this is in your book - we have a note by the military prosecutor, and I always trust legal institutions, even if they are military legal institutions. In his note of 22nd of November, the military prosecutor mentioned the three soldiers and wrote, in black and white, that the soldiers decided of their own free will, initiative, without having received any orders. The military prosecutor - his name is Mladen Jurisic - filed a request for an in-depth investigation. He added that the three soldiers decided of their own initiative, and the prosecutor asked them to be prosecuted. And if you look at it more closely -- I'm sorry if my questions are always lengthy, but I am very cautious and very technical in asking them, and I see that these three soldiers are members of the Convicts Battalion from Siroki Brijeg. But as far as remember, who issued orders to that battalion for positioning men with that tank at that position, and who was in charge of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Convicts Battalion wasn't over there. The tank, I don't know where that -- where it came from, so I can't answer those questions, I really can't. I know that the Convicts Battalion wasn't there. Now, who manned the tank, who these people were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, according to you, the Convicts Battalion wasn't there, but how can you explain the fact that three soldiers of that battalion were there, and not only were they there, but they were in a tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Your Honour, well, I can only speculate. Of course, there was mention made of some money given by someone, but those are all speculations, and I don't wish to enter into speculations of that kind here because I simply don't know. All I know is what I state here, and that is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the name of the commander of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, well, now, for a time the Convicts -- you had the Convicts Battalion and then you had a portion that was anti-terrorist something. A portion of that battalion was led by Andabak, not the one we mentioned but another Andabak. He was a good soldier and it was a decent unit, but Tuta Naletilic had something to do with this particular battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the document, 3D1469, for the first time. If I had known, I would have brought with me the presidential minutes. If I remember correctly - I do have a good memory - in the course of November, after the 9th of November, Mr. Tudjman, who attends a meeting together with a few prominent figures - I assume Susak is there - and President Tudjman asks to have information provided to him concerning the Old Bridge. I am sure I will be able to put the presidential transcripts on the screen. And President Tudjman is aware of that for the first time, and he puts the following question. This is from memory that I quote him. Who ordered the destruction of the Old Bridge? That is the question he puts to the people who are around him. And, strangely enough, there is no answer in the transcript to his question. There is a blank, and someone said there is the noise -- we hear the noise of a piece of paper. As you can see, I have an excellent memory because I remember that one can hear the noise of a piece of paper, so somebody must have provided the answer and said who had given the order, but it is not in the transcript. It would have been interesting to know whether this had been taken off the transcript deliberately, why is somebody ruffling some paper, which makes a noise. But since we never had -- since we don't have the audiotape and since we will never have the audiotape, since they have disappeared, we will never know. General Praljak, in 1997 you write to Mr. Tudjman. Does he answer your letter or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, he invited the three people who are mentioned here because he realised -- well, I don't know what it was all about, but I'm telling you I was labelled as the person who destroyed the bridge. That was generally-accepted truth. It was written in every newspaper, Praljak and the HVO tore down the bridge. And, of course, this bitterness, dismay and anger boiled in me, and that's why I wrote this letter. He invited the three people, and they complained to me afterwards that there was a lot of shouting and screaming going on up there. Nobody completed the investigation, and there were all those stories, rumours, circulating around. Every journalist had his or her interpretation, and they were adding stuff up -- adding stuff, making stuff up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you knew you were going to testify here, since you announced this a long time ago. And since you announced this, a number of years have gone by. In light of the resources you have, even if your resources are limited, why is it that you did not try to contact these three soldiers? Why didn't you ask them who had given them the order to be there on the spot, and why is it that you did not go right up the chain? That was easy enough to do it. It takes, at best, one or two days. You could have done that. Why didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, because two of them were already dead, a long time dead, and I couldn't trace the third one. That's why I am telling you this is a dark story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were detained together with Tuta, didn't you discuss this issue with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't really talk all that much with Mr. Naletilic, not about that at all, and he wouldn't have told me anything even if he knew anything. And we were not on good terms, so apart from some -- you know, the time of day, things of that nature, just basic courtesy, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before we begin, could I ask that we go back to page 25 of the transcript. It's a number of pages ago now. Judge Trechsel had asked the question of the general, whether there was a written order forbidding any shots being fired. That's at line 7, page 25. And then General Praljak's answer is recorded, but it's not attributed to General Praljak. It's still listed as being part of Judge Trechsel's question, that is the words "No, it is not written." And I think that is an error in the transcript, and if so, I would ask that it be clarified or corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I can testify under oath, if need be, that I have not given that answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered by saying that I did not. No written orders are issued for things like that. You talk to people and you tell them, You shouldn't do that, and you explain to them why. That's how it's done. Why should I issue an order not to destroy the Old Bridge? Let me repeat, the Law of War allowed me to destroy the Old Bridge. It was a military facility. And this issue should not be raised before this Tribunal at all. Americans tore down 64 bridges in Serbia, they destroyed them. That was regarding Kosovo. And here I'm talking about the factual truth, and legally it's a totally different thing. I did not destroy it, I did not issue orders for it to be shelled, and this had nothing to do with me. And now, legally speaking, a military facility that is used for offensive operations, well, the Judges will confirm that because they are experts, they know that much better than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, as we have returned to the issue, could you tell the Chamber on what occasion and to whom you gave this oral order that no one should shoot at the Stari Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I walked around the lines at Hum -- I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are receiving French interpretation on the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have interpretation now? So the operational zone commanders, the artillery commanders' questions, that's normal. They see from the photographs -- you can see from the photographs that they can see from above that the military -- that the BH army is using it for military purposes, and they are asking me whether we could fire around the bridge to prevent the supplies being brought in, and I'm telling them, No, no, no. And I repeated that four or five times. I explained to the lads, talking to them, that this was not a military target of such importance that it would warrant the destruction of this piece of cultural heritage with such great architectural and cultural value. And then on the 20th and the 21st, there was a big attack on West and there was a shelling from the Republika Srpska Army positions. No shells were fired on the Old Bridge. Not even then, when I think every soldier in the world would say, Prevent the bringing in of the new troops using this Old Bridge, and I didn't allow it, and my lads obeyed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you remember, the Prosecutor, pursuant to 92 bis, had asked for two statements of citizens from Eastern Germany to be admitted. These people were former mercenaries of the HVO. The Defence had asked to cross-examine both these witnesses, and the Trial Chamber had ordered a decision to say that these two witnesses could come under the condition that they be cross-examined. And the Prosecutor, for reasons that are his own, felt it was not necessary to bring these two German -- East German nationals to testify. At the time, they were still being detained. I remember, however, that one of the two - I don't remember which one - had said that at some point it had been contemplated by the HVO, at the level of the unit he was part of, to go up the river to drop an explosive in that spot, and the plan had been abandoned, given that it was extremely difficult to perform. So any reasonable trier of fact, and I repeat, any reasonable trier of fact, could conclude thereof that a plan had been formed to blow up the bridge. As far as you know, the German mercenaries, had they been given orders to lay mines on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I have no clue as to what they're talking about, what kind of order they could get to shell the bridge. It's 1.800 metres from Stotina, the position where the HVO was, to the bridge, along the Neretva River, and there is the BH Army positions on the other side. Only a fool could say something like that. You have to have American or French special forces who would reach the bridge, pass 1.800 metres up-river to the bridge and set the explosives, and then blow up the bridge. Well, there were dogs of war who perhaps might have thought of something like that, but the Main Staff and we -- and I, as part of the Main Staff, did not allow any fire on the main bridge up until the 9th, when somebody set up the camera and set fire to the fuses and set the explosives on the left bank of the River Neretva. I had nothing to do with it. Six billion people and all the judges of the world, if they were to come to the other side, well, I have nothing to do with the firing with the tank. The HVO has nothing to do with it at any level. Whoever thought that up, whoever cooked that up, this was just a diversion. It was done as part of some great political game, if I may be allowed to speculate, and that was to completely destroy any remnants of the good relations between Muslims and Croats and to charge the HVO and myself personally for some political reasons. But these are speculations, although I could substantiate those claims quite reasonably, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are to follow your theory, namely, that the bridge was destroyed by an explosive under water, as was said, this was done in Mirdo [phoen], which runs parallel to the bridge - we're still waiting to hear this expert witness, Mirdo - how could the Muslims have laid mines on the bridge? They would have to go down into the water. How can you explain this, technically speaking? At night, because during the day everybody could have seen them? How can you explain this, technically speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, first of all, I will not speak about Muslims as a collective noun. Well, those who participated in the conspiracy, I don't know who they were. But, number one, they did not set the explosive in the water, but in the hollow parts of the bridge, and it was only the cable used to activate the explosive, it was left to float down the Neretva River maybe 100 or 150 metres, and then they used the induction detonator to activate the explosives. You can do that in broad daylight, because the banks of the Neretva River are steep and you can't see anything. So only a chance passerby would see that, so it was only chance. And once it was set up, an English soldier set up his camera, filmed it all. He was escorted, as the BH forces tell us themselves, down to Sarajevo, where he was supposed to hand over the tape to the Sarajevo TV, and he simply got on an UNPROFOR plane, flew off, and handed the tape over to the BBC [Realtime transcript read in error "B/C/S"]. So I leave everyone to make their own conclusions, and the only conclusion that I want to say is that the HVO and Slobodan Praljak have nothing to do with that. Now, as to who actually has something to do with that, draw your own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without drawing any conclusions at this stage, you specify, nonetheless, that all of this was organised, that the cameraman had been brought there. He filmed all that. After that, he was escorted away. He was placed aboard an UNPROFOR plane, and his film was handed over to Sarajevo Television. So all of this has to do with manipulation and intoxicating people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I am claiming that this is all a huge manipulation. He never handed the tape over to the Sarajevo TV. All the footage that we have seen here, this was actually rebroadcast from the additional BBC [Realtime transcript read in error "B/C/S"] broadcast. The Sarajevo TV, the Austrian TV, and the snippet -- well, he edited it out for whatever reason, whether there were two explosions or just one explosion. We don't have the full original. He didn't hand it over to the Sarajevo TV. It was simply taken over in the usual way it's done when a TV channel broadcasts something. But this was broadcast the same evening on the 9th of November; not from Sarajevo, but from the BBC [Realtime transcript read in error "B/C/S"].

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be "BBC," not "B/C/S. " And at page 34, line 25, line 11, too, and at page 35, line 6. It's not "B/C/S," it's "BBC."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the famous Scott is not a Scott we see here. The Scott whom you write about, how did you know that his name was Scott in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, in the book that I published, well, I learnt his name afterwards, because I asked a German journalist to get in touch with him, if he could, and try to learn as much as he could about it. It's a gentleman who made a film about the destruction of the Old Bridge. It was shown in Germany, and Austria, and the Netherlands a couple of times. I know the name of this gentleman. He was called "Schotte." That means a Scotsman. So it's not that his name was Scott. He was known as a Scotsman. An English soldier, but he was from Scotland. And this is what the Muslim papers say. That's at -- that's in my book. Let me show you where it is stated -- well, it's in "Oslobodjenje", Thursday, 19th of June, 1997, the Croatian page is 34, where this issue is discussed, and it says a Scotsman trained his camera at the bridge. He was in the town as a member of the British Army. So there were no British people down there, so I find it really strange. I don't know what a British soldier was doing in Mostar when the Spanish soldiers were in charge of that area. And it is said here that on Dudakovic’s orders, this man - and Dudakovic was deputy commander of the 4th Corps - headed to Sarajevo, escorted by the Military Security from the 4th Corps. So this is explicitly stated here. But instead of handing over this precious document, as had been arranged, to the director of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Radio and Television, he managed to get on the first UNPROFOR flight out of Bosnia. This is what the Muslims are writing, not Praljak. So these are their statements quite some time after the actual event, and I can't get -- I couldn't learn anything apart from that. As to what his role was down there, I could give you the name and then perhaps -- well, but it wouldn't serve any purpose, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English page is 3D16-0112. Before we move on, I would like to thank my colleague Mr. Stringer for the correction in the transcript. I wanted to make the same correction myself. It's at line 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before that, I think it was on the 5th of November, we had a meeting in Split; the HVO, Jadranko Prlic, Mate Boban, myself, Petkovic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and so on, where there was a lot of discussion, and in fact President Tudjman asked that we do as much as we can to calm down the tensions with the BH Army to try and find a peaceful solution. Now, as to who actually blew up the bridge and who went against this policy and this conclusion that was generally accepted, well, that goes beyond my ken. I can speculate and make some constructions which I think are quite well founded, but this had nothing to do with the Main Staff, with the HVO command at any level, with myself or with Petkovic. Now, we should go back to the investigation, but two of the people from the tank have been dead for a long time, and I don't know about the third one, whether he's alive or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I want to say that Mr. Mladen Jurisic, that is to say, the person who made the decision to launch an investigation, is now president of the County Court in Mostar and a member of the High Legal Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and according to what the Defence knows, the decision is still with the prosecutor in Mostar -- the case is still with the prosecutor in Mostar and has been there. No progress has been made. They cannot establish the cause for the Old Bridge's destruction, nor can they contact some key witnesses. As we've got just one minute left to the break, I don't want to move on to another area now, which is snipers in Mostar, and I'm sure the general needs more than one minute to deal with that topic. So I suggest we have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. The Trial Chamber is going to hand down a ruling in closed session or private session, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we announced that the next topic for your testimony will be snipers in Mostar and incidents of snipers, sniper fire. Would you like to add anything to what we've already said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the expert on snipers was here, I analysed each of his cases, and I want now to repeat the cases we had here, to go through them briefly. Incident number 1, and the number is 3D00771. I don't have the time to produce the document, but I do claim and state that the gentleman who was wounded in the leg showed how he was standing, he demonstrated that. It is not possible that that wound was caused by fire from the positions at Stotina. That is impossible. It contradicts mathematics. It goes against the grain of maths. And then further on, I say that unfortunately we have seen no medical or police documents to substantiate that. Now, with respect to incident number 2, which I challenged, 3D00756 was the number of the document, and it describes how a nine-year-old was fired at while they were sitting in a water-tank truck. The expert was wrong in determining the location. He was wrong by some 30 kilometres, and the locality that was drawn -- the position of the cistern of the water truck, where it was drawn. And the bullet that shattered the glass, well, I claim that from the position of Stotina, that location cannot be seen optically, and I showed that with the precisely-taken photographs, the photographs I had taken with great precision. Now, as to incident number 3, and I refer to my analysis in 3D00766, it was the case of a woman killed by a shot to the head on the terrace of her house, the experts failed to agree as to whether she was wounded behind her left ear or her right ear. She was found lying on the ground, and I don't see how anyone can establish beyond all reasonable doubt, or beyond any doubt at all, for that matter, that the bullet could have come from Stotina. You can also claim that anybody could have killed her, including her husband. The investigation wasn't completed. With incident number 4, with this street, Marshal Tito Street, I cannot conclude anything on the basis of what was written, so I skip that portion, because there are no elements on the basis of which except arbitrarily to say that the bullet was coming from one side or another. Well, I'm going to skip that one, then. Now, incident number 5, the expert himself says that the victims were in the apartment, so they could not have been visible, and that the house is close to or along the line of the military positions of North Camp, and that most probably it was a case of stray bullets because near that house is where North Camp was situated, which is where the BH Army had its positions and from which there was shooting all the time at HVO lines. Now we come to incident number 6. That was 3D00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Praljak, I have to recall, as I have before, that you are here as a witness. What you are doing now is presenting arguments. From the beginning when you speak on this, you are arguing, you are pleading. And there is a time for that, but this is not the time for pleadings, but the time for witness testimony. You have not been there, you are not an expert, anyway, you do not posit as an expert, so I think that you should not continue in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, I'll accept your guidance. But I'm a super-expert here. As a witness, I can say that what the witness said, in discussing number 6, he took a photograph of the wrong building and said that it was the Staklena Bank or "glass bank," as it was called. This -- well, it wasn't incident number 6, it was another incident. Let me just take a moment to find it. But as a witness, I can say the following. I'm no longer going to testify in this way. As a witness, I can say that in incident number 7, for instance, from the Ledara, the man couldn't have been wounded in the back of his neck, because the angle was coming in at an angle of 90 -- the bullet was coming in at an angle of 90 degrees and not 180 degrees. As a witness, I can also say, with respect to victims number 8 and 14, that there is no optical vision of a single HVO position at the place where these people were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the locality, General, for the record, or could you tell us the page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are victims number 8 and 14, and the incidents took place in Brkic Street by the fire brigade. So as a witness, I'm testifying that there was no visibility, line of vision, either from the Staklena Banka, glass bank building, or any other position where these people were wounded. And as far as incident number 9 is concerned, I would have to present arguments, so I'm going to skip that. But with incident number 10, well, I'll skip that too, because I'm not here to offer up arguments as to why the bullet cannot lodge at an angle of 45 degrees. But with incident number 11, I claim, Your Honours, that the witness on the photograph marked and said -- put down "glass house," whereas that building is not the glass house or glass bank, and I say that under oath. That is not the glass bank building. It is a building that is at least 300 metres away from the glass bank to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you mark that position which you claim is not the glass bank? Could you put that on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The image has to be turned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: 90 degrees, please. That's better, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you have it, Your Honours. The expert wrote here and indicated that this was the glass house or glass bank [indicates]. I claim that that is not right. The glass bank is in this direction over here [indicates], whereas this is another building. It's one of the buildings from the area that is referred to as Centre 2. Here we have an enlargement [indicates], he zoomed in here, but that is wrong. It is information which is not truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, for the record, you indicated the direction in which the glass bank building actually was located. Could you describe that to us in words, for the record?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The glass bank is over here [indicates] or, rather, this is not the glass bank building [marks]. That's not it there. And I'll sign my name down at the bottom [marks]. And it's the 8th today, isn't it? "08/06/2009."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a number, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC1026. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have prepared questions on this victim -- on these victims. I'll only relay the questions -- or seven victims during the time when you were in command until 1993, so I'll ask the questions later. But I have one for now. In these proceedings, each party carries on their own investigation; the Prosecution does and you do, too. This is the way the proceedings work. In order to carry out investigations, you have resources which are granted to you by the Registry. The Registry supplies -- grants financial resources to the Defence parties. Why did you not think of reconstructing, by night with laser rifles, the case by the Prosecution to see the points of origin and the points of impact? I've done that thousands of times when I was working as a prosecutor. It's very easy to do, but you have to have done it at least once in your life. And even if you were not used to it, you could have asked lawyers or experts to reconstruct situations like that for you in order to demonstrate that what the Prosecution expert said was not right. You did not do it. Well, we take what you say into account, but you should have gone by the book. What can you say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, technically speaking this is without fault. It's mathematically, geometrically correct. The distance, visibility, it was done by the book, by the rules. I placed a man in Mostar at the exact position where the event took place, and he was there to film and zoom in to the place from which the expert claims the bullet had come. Then I placed the man in the position where the bullet came from, using a camera, zooming in and out, reducing the angle of the lens, moving towards the location where the man was hit, on the basis of a diagram and a description by the expert describing how the individual stood, where he was facing, and where the bullet was coming from; for example, with the little boy crossing -- running across the road. For each of those individual cases, I used mathematical precision and visual precision to show that that had nothing to do with any reasonable assertion. It's not expertise. I asked the man, Is he ashamed? Well, he said he wasn't ashamed, but I'm ashamed. I ashamed for him, for how he did his work. And I set all this out in my documents. They're precise documents. I think that for one of the cases, I didn't have enough time to go into that, my time had expired, but you can ask me about that and I will clearly show you, using mathematics, that the analysis of the expert just does not hold water, except for the Marshal Tito Street incident, where we can speculate. I don't know. But as to the rest, I have been precise to the very last detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't find the photographs that we attached just now during the expert testimony, all the positions from which it was claimed that the shooting came from in Mostar and the positions where the people who were hit were located. Unfortunately, I don't have the numbers and the photographs, but we did use those photographs and display them during the expert witness testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have them all, but we don't have time. So when Judge Antonetti asks me about this, I'll be able to show him exactly, with mathematical precision. I will show him that the expert did his job -- well, that he couldn't care less how he was going to accomplish his task.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you have anything else on sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, since I don't have -- well, I understand, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, that I can't go on, but I claim that he goes as far as to mark the buildings wrongly, although he had seen it. He really doesn't care. He couldn't care less if he marks its location 100 metres here or 200 metres there, angles, distances, he couldn't care less, line of sights, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There's no reason to fear, Mr. Praljak. I have a very basic and pragmatic question. Haven't these photos and so forth not been presented to the Chamber already? Are they not admitted into evidence? I seem to recall that we have seen a lot of material. So it will not be necessary to send them again, because they are definitely not lost. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now we can go on, Ms. Nika.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can go on. Now I would like the Court Deputy to give 3D03566 to the Judges. Oh, I'm sorry, the general has drawn a map over the weekend that he would now like to show.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, you asked me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- about the positions of the BH Army. I can see -- well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the witness is kindly asked to speak in the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, there's a problem, because when look at the map, your face is turned away from the microphone, so the interpreters have difficulty in understanding you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please repeat the number of the document that this map pertains to? Is this 3D --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you won't be able to see anything from this distance. I would kindly ask that this be handed to the Judges, Their Honours, and to the Prosecution, because you won't be able to see anything. Could you please give this to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we have to try at least for you to show, because we only have one copy, so we can't really distribute it before you've explained.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours and the Prosecution, according to the document we have written down the numbers indicating locations. This is the translation into English, and I signed it [indicates]. Your Honours, I think - and the translators also note this - there is a mistake. The figures in the English and the Croatian did not tally by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A suggestion to the technician. Could not the camera be zoomed on this map? Then perhaps we can see more.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, this pertains to the locations in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mostar [indicates]. This is Northern Camp [indicates], the Tihomir Misic barracks, number 1, and here we have the BH Army and the HVO lines that are drawn in [indicates]. And now, because of the number of positions, we marked the positions in Santiceva and the Spanish Square, and here around the Old Bridge and Cernica [indicates], the position that are listed in the document, and the positions at Stotina and the machine-gun emplacement that is facing Stotina, and so on [indicates].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we want to understand better, because we are at least 20 metres away from the map. We have little white squares in the map. What do they mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The small white squares indicate -- well, here you have the legend, number 1, number 1, number 2, number 2 here [indicates], and we have the translation in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, perhaps for the record, you could at least tell us what number 1 is. Is that a BH Army position, in a street, in the town, in a house; what is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, well, we've drawn this in about 30 times already. This is the Tihomir Misic barracks, the Northern Camp where the BH Army was, and here you have the lines that are drawn in and everything else [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
