utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, you have the pointer. Use it to show us precisely where the Northern Camp is, or the North Camp, because you keep moving the pointer, so it's hard to follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So say number 1 is the North Camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the other numbers, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 1 is the Northern Camp. Number 2 -- and then it just goes on all the way through to 23. A square corresponds to the number that is listed here, and we have the English translation indicating the identity of each location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us quickly what these 23 sites represent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-three locations indicate the sniper positions, unit positions, machine-gun nests of the BH Army at the separation line with the HVO. In fact, it's only number 3, Your Honours, which is Stotina, it's the HVO position at Stotina which we have mentioned so many times before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you know that these were BH Army positions? What do you have to be able to claim this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the document that we looked at last week. First of all, I know that these were BH Army positions, because I was quite well aware of it, but this was drawn on the basis of the document, the document that you asked me about. You, yourself, asked me why I didn't draw a map, because the map that the author appended to the original document is gone, it's disappeared, and now, on the basis of the document, I drew this map, I made those markings. But it's undoubtedly accurate, because I know that as an eye-witness of the events; not with, of course, 100 per cent precision for each and every position, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is 3D00929. It's the intelligence report dated the 11th of November, 1993, and we saw it last week.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: September.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. General, now I would like you to take -- okay. Before we that, Mr. Kovacic has warned me that we have to ask for an IC number for this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. An IC number for this map, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The map shall be given Exhibit IC1027. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you surprise us here because we did not expect to do this work, but when I look at the positions of the BH Army just off the cuff, I sense that from the position where any BH Army sniper was, he could basically hit any target in Mostar. Is this so or is this wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not any target because of the buildings, but they could target any HVO position. All HVO positions were exposed to the BH Army fire, all the buildings that you can see, everything that you have the line of sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I shall revisit this, but I want this to be clear already. As I understand, your case is that among the people wounded or killed, casualties attributed by the Prosecutor to the HVO, your case is that the victims could have been BH Army's victims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is correct, but I am, in fact, claiming just one thing with 100 per cent certainty, and that is the following: The explanation of the expert, that such and such a man who was injured by the HVO sniper, as he claims, well, that's not true. That's what I'm saying with full certainty. The explanations that are provided by the expert, that, for instance, in Brkica Street, two men were shot, this is not true, because there is no line of sight from any HVO positions to that site, and so on. And if you recall, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I asked a witness who was a victim, I asked him, Sir, do you ask yourself to this day who actually fired at you? And he responded, Yes, General. He's an old man and he knows to this day that -- what he has been told, that he was shot by the HVO, that this is not true. He knows that the position where he was shot cannot be seen from the glass bank. And then the expert says, Well, there could have been a mobile sniper position in a square which is completely open. Well, this is something -- really something, to say that there is a mobile sniper position, somebody just driving around, and the BH Army positions are 50 metres away, and all those buildings. Well, it really begs belief and it's an insult to logic. It's really an insult to basic human logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I would now like to ask you to look at 3D03566. It's a book, "Government of Democratic Unity of the Republic of Croatia." Now I would like you to explain to Their Honours, first of all, who authored this book and what the author's function was, and what was the function of the Government of Democratic Unity, and then we will go on through the book itself, and go through it highlighting important elements.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the book itself was, in a way, edited or put together by a journalist, Milovan Baletic, but the actual editor, the person who approved it, who worked on it, was the prime minister of the Republic of Croatia in 1991-1992, Franjo Greguric. The Government of National Unity was set up at the proposal of Dr. Franjo Tudjman, not as a government that is put together by the party that won the elections, but this was the government that in those difficult times, when Croatia was on the brink of disappearance, it was barely surviving, the best representatives from all the parties, regardless of their results in the elections, became part of that government, and that is why it was called the Party of Democratic Unity in Croatia. But I would just like to highlight some things to show to Their Honours, the Judges, that the same policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, the international treaties, respect for all the rights, the advocacy of Croatian interests at various conferences by the prime minister and the foreign ministers, that this policy -- also by the Parliament of the Republic of Croatia and the Government of the Republic of Croatia, the president of the state has -- was consistent, this policy, to the effect that Bosnia was an independent state and that it should be helped to survive, in military terms, too, through proposals, as you will see, on economic relations. The only thing that was always brought up was that in accordance with the proposals of the international community, this state should be internally organised in such a way that three constituent peoples should be happy with the way it is set up, so that the peoples who live in that state should not feel that they're short-changed or at a disadvantage in any way. There should be a mirror-image symmetry. And that's all I have to say about it. It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment. For record, when you say "that state," and we just have the Republic of Croatia written in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the one that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give us the page number?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 107 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And that is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In e-court, it is page 3D41-1285, in Croatian, and for the English it is 3D41-0379 and 3D41-0380.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vice-premier, Dr. Zdravko Tomac, who was a social democrat otherwise, informed the Government of the Republic of Croatia about talks between the Croatian delegation and the delegation of the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They said that the action of the armed forces should be prohibited from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina towards Croatia because there was an enormous aggression and Bosnia-Herzegovina was, not through the will of its own government, but through the impotence of its own government and the impotence of its president, the president of the Presidency, Izetbegovic, who wasn't standing up to the Yugoslav People's Army in opposition. So it was an aggression against Croatia. And if we look at the states, this state was attacking the Republic of Croatia. Now, who was doing the attacking? Either one state attacking another or it was the JNA aggression, but then we don't have a state because they were attacking everyone, because they thought that all this should be in the frameworks of a Greater Serbia. So the principle is that either we have states, and then Bosnia-Herzegovina is the aggressor in that case, if that's the truth, or states do not exist in that shape and form, and then the aggressor is the JNA and Greater Serbia. So that's it, there we have it. And then it goes on to say that it's difficult -- the situation is difficult in Kostajnica, Sisak, Dubica, Petrinja, and so on and so forth. I was in Sisak. I know about all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what time are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we can move on to page 151, and we're dealing with the 30th of September, page 151.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It is 3D41-1288, for the Croatian, and the English is 3D41-0380.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we'll have a look at this, since you are showing this, but I had a question this weekend and I felt it was important. You've just told us that there was a national unity government. Fine. What I'd like to know is this: At the time, was there an opposition? Did everybody agree 100 per cent with Mr. Tudjman, and they supported him, or was there a form of opposition, and if so, who were the people opposing the government? I'm asking you this question because contrary to what I thought initially, I thought that Mr. Praljak is a military man, he doesn't know much about political affairs, and I realised over time that you were also a player on the political stage, so my question is a question of a political nature. Was there a form of opposition to the Government of National Unity of Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An exact answer would be just one party was in opposition, and that was the Croatian Party of Rights. It had the HOS, H-O-S, and you saw in the documents that there were a lot of problems there to disarm them. All the other parties -- well, that was a small party, that Party of Rights, with just 6 or 7 per cent of the electorate. It just managed to get through. All the other parties were in the Government of National Unity, and there was no opposition to the policy and politics waged because it was based on a national consensus of Parliament, the Government, and the president of the republic, according to the basic elements: Independence; defence from the aggression; human rights, as you saw over there; maximum national rights, ethnic rights for the Serbs, cultural autonomy for the Serbs if they desired it within Croatia; recognition of the borders of the republic with the disintegration of the former country, Yugoslavia; an attempt at reaching a military agreement on joint defence with Bosnia-Herzegovina. So pure democracy, the rule of law. Anybody transgressing will have to be held responsible. And I'll show you a document from 1992, I'll show you the document that I wrote myself. So it was national consensus at this point, both of the parties and the citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So there was a national consensus, but there was the Croatian Party of Rights, the HOS, which represented, according to what you have said - I'm looking at the transcript - 6 to 7 per cent of the general electorate. You'll have at least one week to think about this. I'm not going to put this question directly to you now. But as part of the questions I'm going to put to you on the joint criminal enterprise and on the Banovina, I would like to know whether, in the Croatian Constitution, the Banovina is mentioned. In Croatia, were there people who criticised this? In my country, if I were to try this kind of case, I would have read everything and I would know everything back to front, but in this case I don't read and understand the Croatian language, and I don't know if articles were published that criticised the Banovina. When I put questions to you about this subject, I'd like you to tell me whether articles were written at the time about this. This would be of interest to me when I put my question. Thank you. So reflect on this, please, but don't answer straight away. This is not the time. Ms. Pinter, I'll give the floor back to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. General, let me just give the right page number for the record. In English it is 3D41-0380. We've already given the Croatian page number, which is 3D41-1288.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Briefly, it says here that Dubrovnik was being attacked from Trebinje, which is of course in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that it was being attacked from Montenegro via territory -- both BH territory and -- well, they were targeting Dubrovnik, so Bosnia-Herzegovina was the territory from which Dubrovnik was being attacked. And this follows on from the question of what happens with the south, when we raised the question of whether the Croatian Army will have to enter into the depth of BH territory, because you cannot liberate Dubrovnik and free them from fire from that area. I read about this. It's called the tactical depth, the right of entry into a neighbouring country to use tactical depth; that is to say, that you can't target the town using artillery. Anyway, let's move on to page 157 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-1289 is the Croatian number, and in English it is 3D41-0381, for the English. And the English number refers to the next date that follows. Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the prime minister -- or, rather, the president says that they have decided to send a demand -- a request to the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It always says "Government," it always says "Bosnia-Herzegovina," so Judge Antonetti, there's no Banovina. Well, let me answer. Anyway, what it says here -- what are they going to ask for? That the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina undertake everything in its power to stop the unlawful use of the state territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, Bosnia-Herzegovina has state territory, and that state territory is called "Bosnia-Herzegovina," and that's what the prime minister says, and that this state territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina should cease to be used for attacks on the Republic of Croatia by aggressor units. So that's the request that is being made here. There's no need to go into that any further. We can move on. Yes, the next page is 171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Praljak, the attack on Dubrovnik, well, I'm not very familiar with this, apart from the judgement rendered in the Strugar case. I'm no specialist in this field, so I apologise. I apologise for this beforehand. This is a rather innocent question on my part, but bearing in mind what you've just said, you've said two important things: A, that the artillery was surrounding Dubrovnik and the artillery was shelling the town; but, B, you said that you did not cross Bosnia-Herzegovina to get to Dubrovnik to support them there. At the time, did you have any aircraft with which you could have shelled the Serb artillery --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when you were in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Croatia at that time did not have aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a navy with which you could have shelled at the Serb positions from the sea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire navy of the Yugoslav People's Army was taken away by the Yugoslav People's Army to Montenegro. It took the navy with it. So at that time, we didn't have a single warship. The guys around Dubrovnik had those fast speedboats, and despite the blockades set up by the JNA Navy, they managed to bring in some food and ammunition to Dubrovnik, with casualties, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of the attack on Dubrovnik by the Serbs, the Republic of Croatia had how many operational brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, well, what can I say? We're dealing with 1991? What do you say? Well, Your Honour, I think that there was about, on the battle-front, not more than 40.000 volunteers, four brigades of the National Guards Corps and some other brigades, but not more than 40.000 manpower over the whole front, the whole theatre of operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, the page was 3D41-1294 in the Croatian, and for the English it was 3D41-0385, or page 10 of the translation. I think it will be easier for us to find our way that way.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're dealing with the 6th of October here, and that was the time when all of Croatia was burning. We see an overview of all the fighting in Croatia. It says that the European Community had threatened Yugoslavia with a blockade if they continued to ignore the truce and cease-fire. "The warring parties," that was a terrible phrase. We weren't warring parties, we were the victims of aggression, whereas it saying -- the phrase that was used all the time was "warring sides," as if, if I stopped, the Yugoslav People's Army stopped. It didn't, it carried on attacking. So these diplomatic phrases, this one being a case in point, "warring sides," they were an insult to people fighting at that time, but never mind. Dubrovnik is mentioned again, and air attacks, and everything that was set on fire. We needn't deal with that anymore. We can move on to page 191 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The Croatian page is 3D41-1295, and the English is -- I think you've got the page wrong, General. It's not page 191, it's 201.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the interpreters, this is 3D41-1298 for the Croatian, and the English is page 11, or 3D41-0386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving on, General Praljak, a while ago you made a comment on the fact that the international community talked about the warring parties, these are the words you used when you were saying that you were the victims of this. This is your version, but you know full well that the Serbs say the opposite, that they were the victims because you were the aggressors. So there is an issue here. Let me just give you one example. Borovo Selo, each of the parties says the other party is responsible. Do you agree with this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't agree with that, either with you or with the Serb side, Judge Antonetti. Borovo Selo was the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and in Borovo Selo, people were captured, and the police of the Republic of Croatia had the right to intervene in Borovo Selo. And according to the socialist constitution and the JNA, no, it didn't. What we saw in Dubrovnik, what we saw in Vukovar, what we saw in Sisak, what I experienced, there were no warring parties or factions. You had the aggressor and you had the victim. And we can open a discussion of whatever kind you want here and hold a debate, but Croatia did not attack Serbia or Bosnia-Herzegovina or Montenegro. I did not go to war with Belgrade. I did not go to fight in Tuzla, Sarajevo, Bihac, and so on. I was defending myself. Wherever I was, all I did was to defend, everywhere. The HVO defended itself, and the Croatian Army defended itself, and I defended myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are mixing up two terms. One is the term of "aggressor" and the other is a term of "belligerent party." As I understand it, a belligerent party is a party that is involved in war, irrespective of whether it is just defending or attacking. "Aggressor" is probably what you refer to, but that is not the word used here, so I wonder whether your criticism is really justified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully understand your remark, and it is true that there are two sides in every war and that you could term them "belligerent parties" or "warring parties." But when Hitler is marching in France, then you cannot call on both belligerent parties or warring factions to stop, because the French Resistance doesn't have anything to stop in -- Guderian's, Rommel's, and divisions have something to stop, and what is at issue here is that they are saying, Stop. Who is to stop? The party who has 1.000 tanks or I, in Sunja, with two mortars? I would have stopped at any point, but provided that what the international law decreed, that Croatia is an independent state, with its borders, its constitution, and let them move out and we will stop. Franjo Tudjman and all of us, we didn't ask for anything more than that. That's all we asked for and the only question is who can stop the war. There are warring sides, belligerent parties, but within that term you also have the aggressor. Germany is an aggressor, Poland is not, in World War II, and Poland -- there is nothing Poland can stop. It was a belligerent party for one month and then it ceased to be a belligerent party because the German troops trampled all over it, as they did France. And then those who fought, the French Resistance, became a belligerent party, but it simply wanted the other guys to go home, where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, the page that we opened, I assume that this pertains to this part the initiative by Montenegro Assembly rejected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And here this is all about what kind of borders we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is crystal clear. The initiative by the Montenegrin Assembly is, Let's agree, let's determine the borders between Croatia and Montenegro by mutual agreement. Why? Because they managed to capture the territory all the way up to Dubrovnik and now they would like to get the mutual agreement. So they do not recognise the borders of the republic as the borders of the newly-emerged states, and they say, Well, we managed to take -- well, you can look at the map, Your Honours, if you please. This is the border of the Republic of Croatia at Prevlaka [indicates], and they managed to take all this area all the way up to Dubrovnik, and now they say the Assembly decided that there should be a mutual agreement about the borders. Of course, the government and the president and the Parliament of the Republic of Serbia rejected the initiative, because we didn't want to have any mutual agreements about borders that were established by aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, but this speaks to the attitude of the government towards changing of the borders?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it says the government will persist on the fact that there cannot be changes of the internal borders of the former SFRY and rejected the possibility of any talks, so they ruled out the possibility of any talks about the borders changing, the borders of the republics that have now emerged; no Banovina, nothing can be changed in this regard. There is a way in which you can change it. Once the war is over, once everything is over, and then for some reason somebody says, We would like to change something by peaceful means. When two parties agree peacefully, of course you can change. That's how it's done in Europe, and this is enshrined in the Conference on European Security and Cooperation. But there can be no changing of borders by force, and this is what we were dealing with, but not by the Republic of Croatia, which has always had the same attitude. The changing of the borders is not at issue. This cannot even be broached as a topic, so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. Page 285, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it's page 13 in the English translation. E-court pages are 3D41-1305 and 3D41-0388.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if this has been translated or not. Just a couple of things. So on that date, I can read, and I quote: "The Assembly of Serbia rejected the Brussels Declaration --"

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And can you remember what else happened on that date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the fall of Vukovar. And I quote: "The Serbian Assembly rejected the Brussels Declaration on the recognition of sovereignty of all the republics of the former Yugoslavia who wish to have their sovereignty recognised." So the Brussels Declaration was rejected by Serbia and by Montenegro, but it was accepted by Croatia; there can be no changes to the borders. And I will go on repeating it. I know that by heart. These are political projects that stem from the 1970s or 1980s. We never wanted to change any borders. All we wanted to have was Croatia. And then he goes on to say that -- well, it is stated that the Croatian Community of HZ was set up, and the purpose is to respect the democratic government in Bosnia-Herzegovina for as long as there is the independence of -- for as long as Bosnia-Herzegovina is independent of any Yugoslavia in any shape and form. So that was the political position of that community and of the Croatian people. So Bosnia and Herzegovina is recognised, as is its democratically-elected government, unless that government, without first seeking the opinion of the Croatian people, wants to join Yugoslavia together with the Serbs. And I didn't want that. I don't know what the others would do, but as a member of a sovereign people, that was my right, to say that I don't want that. "Yes" to sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, "yes" to its democratically-elected government, but "no" to the government which would sell itself to a Serbia and to the Yugoslav People's Army for -- to serve the interests of one single people, be it Serbs or Muslims. And that, Your Honours, is the basic problem that you must understand if you want to understand the position, the desires of the HZ-HB and the Croatian people. And we keep dancing about it and beating around the bush 100 times, "yes" to Bosnia-Herzegovina, a unified democratic state, but we as a people, nobody can sell us down the river. Let us move on, Ms. Nika.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We have a note here, "Resolution 724 is accepted," at page 341. Shall we go to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's at page 14 of the English translation. It's 3D41-1389, and the Croatian is 3D41-1308.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, sorry for interrupting you. I've just realised one thing, looking at this book. In the B/C/S version, there are parts that are not complete, so you selected some parts and we don't have some B/C/S pages. Secondly, you have translated certain pages which you selected. The reason why I'm asking you this is that I was interested in what Mr. Greguric said when -- that the HZ-HB was created on the 18th of November in Grude. I sought to understand how, in the matter of government, Croatia assisted in this. On page 13 of the English version, you said that this community -- well, not you, but Mr. Greguric said that the community was established, but we do not know what the context was, and it would have been interesting to know whether there had been discussions in the Croatian government or whether this was a fait accompli. Did they sort of guide all this remotely, as is suggested by the Prosecution case? You give us a small tidbit of it, but this does not enlighten us on the interest from the point of view of the Croatian government, when the HZ-HB was created. Did you realise that when you only cherry-picked, you exposed yourself to some criticism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I'm well aware of that, but please believe me when I say that I would be really happy -- and this is what I have been thinking about, an idea that I have been toying with, the whole book that was published by these two on behalf of the Government of National Unity, to have it translated in full, because this would give you an overview, and if the Prosecution or if anyone else wants to do that, well, that would make me really happy. It was only for lack of resources that I had to cherry-pick some parts, and this shows the consistency of the Croatian policies, state and so on, and there was no collusion between the Government of National Unity and the HZ-HB. We, down there, we were a people. We're not somebody's dwarves. We asked for the weapons -- for assistance in weapons, and so did Alija Izetbegovic and the other -- and the BH Army to a much greater extent. But we were alone down there and we managed to defend ourselves. But I would be more than happy if a party -- if somebody managed to find a detail in this book, and I'm also asking the Prosecutor to do that, to prove whether my choice was meant to hide something, to conceal something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, on the 18th of November, when the Croatian Community was created in Grude, I guess that the Croatian press spoke about it in Zagreb. It could have been very easy for you to read the Croatian press to prove that this creation had nothing to do with the Republic of Croatia, that the HZ-HB was created ex nihilo, that it is something that was created by the municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not by Croatia, and you could have adduced as evidence such press clippings. You could also have researched, in the intelligence services, documents made known to the government to the effect that in the neighbouring republics, some municipalities had agreed in order to create a Croatian community, and this could -- may have given rise to problems in the future. I mean, this type of information was around, it was not in the Middle Ages in 1991, but you give us very little evidence, but for the odd article from a book that we do not have in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I have really striven so hard to prove my innocence, it goes beyond any border. What is it that the Prosecution must do, then? There were no conquests in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the press or outside of the press, with the government or without the government, with President Tudjman or without President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I agree with you, the onus of proof lies on the Prosecution, but you know we have a two-tier proceeding here. We have the Prosecution case, and then you have, at the same time, the Defence case. Of course, you could just sort of do nothing, but you do have a part to play, and as part of this role which is yours, unfortunately, sir, you have to prove that you are innocent, and doing so can be done by way of press articles in Zagreb at the time the HVO was created, or evidence from the intelligence services showing that all this happened in Herzegovina without any contact whatsoever with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, at the -- I was actually at the Military Council, in the Council of National Defence. I was the assistant minister, I received all the secret reports, so why should I, given that there are five statements by the government and 50 statements by Franjo Tudjman, why should I go through press articles? I knew what we were saying, what we were doing up until, well -- and now I am supposed to go to newspapers to look for what Miroslav Medjimorec, who was the head of the SIS, and he was also a very good director, to see what he's doing, and I know what he's doing. In the previous text, and Franjo Tudjman says, Don't go towards Trebinje, where is this damn Trebinje here somewhere, to liberate the south of Croatia. So when he's talking about conquering Bosnia, that's what he's talking about. He doesn't even allow the units to go into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I do not disagree with what you're saying, but the problem is as follows: You say that you were in this Council of National Defence, but the problem is that you are an accused here. Even if the presumption of innocence prevails, you are in the situation of an accused. Unfortunately, Tudjman has passed away, but he's taken as being part of the joint criminal enterprise. So if you had any other evidence that came from, in quotation marks, "independent sources," intelligence reports, reporting about political problems in other countries to the authorities, well, the authors of such reports can be assumed to do their work without any bias, and that can be taken into account. Because you say that you are under oath, of course we can believe you, but do not forget that you are an accused here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, Your Honour, this is a government that is composed of all the parties in the Republic of Croatia, all the parties, this government, and now the papers can only report on what the prime minister has said or the prime minister who is from the SDP, or a deputy prime minister who is from the Liberal Party? This government is taking positions. It is representing the Republic of Croatia and its policies. So is this parliament, and so is Franjo Tudjman. My positions partially reflect the positions of the Republic of Croatia. So what should I do? Some journalists who discuss something, well, I could have done that, and we saw that in "Hrvatski Vojnik," "The Croatian Soldier." In "Hrvatski Vojnik," you have an official overview of the Croatian policy, and the journalists who did not work for other papers, Butkovic and others, so these were sociology teachers and specialising in war, so this is the legitimacy of what we say, urbi et orbi. This is the policy of the Republic of Croatia, of all its levels of government. So there can be no changing of the borders, and you will see further on that the Serbs say that they also do not recognise the Brussels Declaration about the borders. Well, I simply don't know what can be done. It was only the HSP, the Croatian Party of Rights, that claimed that Muslims were Croats, and there were Muslims who claimed the same thing and that there should be a state -- Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as a single state. And they got 6 per cent of the vote, and they were not in the government and nobody really -- well, in the end, other opinions must be represented, but these are -- this is the position of the three key bodies in the state, the government, the parties and the president, and I don't really feel any need to go through the newspapers to see if anyone objected or whatever, and the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So when I cross into Bosnia and Herzegovina, I become a Croat born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then I defend the interests. And at that point it is immaterial to me what Greguric would think about it. Greguric could think this or he could think that, and we don't dare -- we're smart enough to say, Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes, we will not attack anyone, but we have the right, as a people, we have our rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to stop here. If I understand, probably the reason why you submit this book is to say that this is illustrative of the policy of the Croatian government, and as to the events in 1991, 1992 and 1993, this shows the vision of the Croatian government, which is or was, as you reminded us, a government of national unity. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could make one brief comment. I'm looking at page 68 of the transcript, back around line 10, where the President indicated, at least in the transcript, that the general has a role to play and that he has to prove that he's innocent. I don't know whether the President intended to say it just that way or not. I'm a little bit uncomfortable with that remaining on the record as it is, without it being clarified. It's certainly not the Prosecution position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to clarify. I said that in the proceedings in this Tribunal, both parties play a part; the Defence has a part to play, and so has the Prosecution. The Prosecution charges, and the Defence defends itself, and as part of this role, there might be a part to be played by the accused, but he also can decide to do nothing. It is his choice. Is it clear now, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I believe so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We wanted to react to that page of the transcript because we were aware of the fact that there might be a mistake. But looking at the clock now, are we going to go on or shall we going to take a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can break for 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You wanted the floor, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just very briefly, I hope. And I don't know whether the general's going to finish his direct testimony today or not, but as we transition out of his direct testimony into the questions that will be coming from the President and then from the other Defence teams on cross-examination, and then from the Prosecution, we went back, and it's been a long time now, but on the 5th of September, 2008, the Appeals Chamber issued its decision affirming or upholding a decision of this Trial Chamber which granted the Praljak Defence the ability to continue to communicate with General Praljak throughout the time that he's testifying. That was an issue that was raised a long time ago, and the Trial Chamber agreed or ruled that the contact and the communications could, indeed, continue between General Praljak and his counsel throughout his testimony. That was upheld. I wanted to ask or to clarify my understanding that now, as we move beyond direct examination, that the general will be free to continue to communicate with his Defence team and to, for example, review the documents that are disclosed in advance to the Defence prior to the cross-examination. It would be useful to know whether, in fact, that is something that is going to be taking place as the documents are disclosed to the Praljak Defence that will be used in the coming cross-examination or whether, indeed -- and I don't know whether, Mr. President, whether you're intending to use documents and circulate those in advance, but whether, in fact, they'll have the opportunity to review those with their client in advance of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two things in what you said. You mentioned Praljak's discussions with his Defence lawyers, and you mentioned the documents. As far as I'm concerned, I will send you tomorrow already the list of documents I am going to show General Praljak. These documents have all been admitted already. Therefore, I'm not disclosing anything new. Nothing mysterious about these. They are two series of documents. The first series is the series mentioned in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief, which you're familiar with. Since these are documents which contain footnotes, nothing unexpected. The second things I will address are the documents that have been quoted by Mr. Praljak, and I will give a list of these documents. Prior to that, there will be four or five documents I shall look at together with him. These are documents which relate to the so-called forged documents. I mentioned one a while ago, but I shall examine these so-called forged documents. I will also address the issue of presidential transcripts, those meetings which he attended. You have the list of all the transcripts of the meetings he attended. This will depend on the amount of time I have. I will also address the presidential transcripts of the meetings he did not attend. We have evidence that leads us to believe that Mr. Tudjman was kept informed in realtime of all the events that occurred in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; namely, any event of a military nature, as part of the international conflict or as part of the joint criminal enterprise. So you will be getting the list of all these documents, which everyone is familiar with already, since they have been discussed and addressed and admitted. Now, as far as the second part is concerned, i.e., whether Mr. Praljak and his counsel can talk together, we must confer. I cannot give you my answer straight away. And since we have eight days before us, you will certainly have a decision by the Trial Chamber between then and now. Are you satisfied with my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the remaining time we have, one hour, please try to finish, Ms. Pinter. We have exactly one hour left, so finish with those documents you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour, and I do believe that we'll be able to complete the examination-in-chief by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, let's deal with the document that we were dealing with before the break, to finish that off so that we can go on to another area.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 341, there's just a sentence there, that Dr. Franjo Tudjman sent a peace mission to the United Nations or, rather, a letter of peace, reminding them once again that Croatia was in favour of peace and understanding and cooperation. So that was one of a series of documents sent out explaining Croatia's position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And we've already looked at that page before the break; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can move on, then, and the number of the page is 419 for the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's page 15 of the English translation. On e-court, it's 3D41-0390, and in Croatian it is 3D41-1317.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just briefly, Croatia recognised the Republics of Slovenia and Macedonia. Croatia is paying particular attention - we're dealing with the 15th of February here - is following the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina with great attention, and there was an agreement offered up in order to promote international cooperation. Croatia supports the referendum and the agreement reached by the three ethnic groups. And if there was a positive outcome of the referendum, it would recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina. It can't be clearer than that. So let's move on now to 460 -- 435 is the next page, actually. My mistake. That wasn't translated. Well, let's have 460, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is 3D41-0393 for the English and 3D41-1348 for the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Part of page 435 was in fact translated. We have a passage on page 3D41-0391.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right. Greguric informed the government about the events and development in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, linked to the referendum on independence and autonomy, and it's important to mention here that the Presidency of BH accepted the majority of the requests of the Serbian Democratic Party and stated, the Presidency of BH, that is, that the referendum held does not preempt a future system and setup for Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was always a question of the internal system for BH, with assurances given that the referendum still did not say what Bosnia-Herzegovina was to look like, internally speaking, and we know what their wishes were. So can we look at 460 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just explain to Judge Trechsel it was my mistake. I skipped a page. Now page 460 is 3D41-1348, and for the English it is 3D41-0393.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Judge Trechsel kindly switch his microphone off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Page 18 is the next page we're going to deal with now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same old story, repeated parrot fashion. Greguric is saying that Croatia was always in favour of an integral BH because it considers that to be the only solution for that republic. This does not mean that there was a lack of care for Croats in BH. Next this story about the HSP to the Drina, he said this was all stupid, and he was speaking in his own name, and that that wasn't official Croatian policy, and he says the government will propose that Croatia recognise BiH. And he goes on to say that what the Serbs were doing was up to the consciousness of the international community and that they should not be indifferent to observing a repetition of the Croatian scenario, that is, the breaking up of the country. So I have nothing to add there, and we can move on to 469, please, of the 17th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's page 18 of the English translation. On e-court, it is 3D41-1351 for the Croatian and 3D41-0393 for the English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia, Slovenia and Georgia were accepted as members of the OSCE, CSCE, and Dr. Mato Granic called upon the European Community to recognise BH and Macedonia as sovereign and independent states. So that's the policy. The Croatian representative is calling upon the members of the European CSCE, the CSCE. And we can move on to page 507.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-165 [as interpreted] is the Croatian and 3D41-0398 is for the English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8th of April, 1992. It is the government statement about the situation in BH --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I have to give the numbers. I apologise for interrupting. They are 3D41-1365 for the Croatian and 3D41-0398 for the English, and the page is 23 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The introductory address of the government about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina took place, and all the ministers then took part in the debate. And the text of the statement of the Croatian government on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was accepted, but that hasn't been translated. Can we supply a translation subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's an eight-point document of crystal-clear points, representing the positions of the Government of the Republic of Croatia about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina; what is being recognised, what the stands and principles are, set out in eight points which, on the 8th of April, were compiled; recognition of an independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina; genocide is already being mentioned. The conclusions of Parliament in point 2 are mentioned, the Croatian Parliament, the Croatian parliamentary conclusions; all the houses sitting and held on the 27th of March, 1992, where the president was advised that he recognise the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which the president did on the 7th of April, 1992. And in point 3, there is talk of mutual recognition for Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, international recognition - I misspoke - of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is welcomed by the government. The government welcomes international recognition, the United States recognition, and so on. And in point 5, the government once again lends its support to the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and condemns destabilisation attacks and so on and so forth. Please have that text translated, because it's crystal clear, speaks for itself, and we have had umpteen similar texts. So if you could have it translated so that Their Honours can admit it into evidence. And we can go on to page 542, which does not have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the date is --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, before we move on to page 542, I would like to still look at pages 506 and 507. On page 506, Mr. Greguric says that the Republic of Croatia recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina unilaterally as a sovereign and independent state. This is mentioned in the text. And on the 8th of April, he says what follows, and I believe this is interesting. He says that the HVO was set up as a sole institution to defend the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This includes a number of Muslims. He mentions the HVO. He doesn't say that it's the Republic of Croatia that created the HVO. He says -- well, if what he says is true, I don't know. He says that. And at the same time, he talks about the HOS, so he seems to establish a connection with the role played by the HOS in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What do you have to say to this? You've seen this. I don't have the entire page 507 translated. What does Mr. Greguric mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 506? Ah, 507, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The 8th of April is the date.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 8th of April. Now, Your Honour, as to the spring of 1992, we've discussed that at great length. The HVO self-organised itself for defence, not only for the defence of the Croats, but of the Muslims, too, living on the territory where we managed to set up our units to resist the aggression, and Greguric is reporting to the government about that. There are armed forces over there defending Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's it, Muslims and Croats alike. And now we have the problem of HOS, the H-O-S, and there was a major problem in Croatia until the authorities and government became stabilised in that destructive war that we had down there, and we solved it all together, throughout 1992, until the problem was solved, until the units of HOS, as a parallel army, and I've already spoken about that. But we managed to deal with the situation, both with Mr. Prkacin, who was from the HOS, who came to understand that it was all we could do to face the problems of one army, and now that when there are two armies --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The Judge was asking about the 8th of April because it wasn't translated. What else does it say under the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what point?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, not the decision, but the 8th of April, as a whole, that whole section in the book. The 8th of April on page 507, is what the Judge is asking about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it says that Croatia called upon the CSCE, et cetera, to stop the aggression against Croatia, and that the HVO was the sole institutional form of defence, including a certain number of Muslims. Resistance to the Serb aggression became more organised in that way. And the members of the Croatian Party of Right formed the Croatian Defence Alliance, the HOS, and then it says that the BiH Presidency only then proclaimed -- sounded the alarm and said that Siroki Brijeg and Citluk were shelled and that the Chetniks attacked Kupres. We've already discussed that. And that in Sarajevo, from the Greater Serbia bombing, 30 people were killed in the space of one week; that the United States of America condemned Serbia for expanding the war to BH. And it says the Ministry of the Republic of Croatia calls upon the pilots of the Yugoslav People's Army to join Croatian military units. So that's it, that's what he says under the 8th of April. And then it goes on to elaborate the government positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. We can get back to --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you believe that this part of the book might be useful, at the end of this page there is the statement of the government, the declaration of the government, about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you can see what the position of the Government of the Republic of Croatia was towards Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign, independent state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would really like this to be translated. It is a really important document. I thought we had had it translated and then it could be submitted to Their Honours, the Judges. And this is very clear and set out in eight clear points. So now I would like to ask you if you can go to the next document. It's the only document remaining. That's page 542. Oh, no, we don't have 542.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 6th of April or 7th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, we don't really have to. It's always one and the same thing. But let's -- well, do you have 552, and that would be the last thing, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's page 29 in the English translation; e-court, pages 3D41-0404; Croatian, 3D41-1386. The date is the 14th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the government, yet again, after a debate issues a press release, a communique, and it is important to note once again in paragraph 1 they speak about human and ethnic rights, indicating that the government would support the position of the European Community vis-a-vis Serbia, and asks the governments to respect Croatia's territorial integrity, the Serbian government. And then in item number 2, Bosnia and Herzegovina is discussed, saying that Croatia was among the first to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state within its existing borders. Then it goes on to speak about the refugees that Croatia has taken in, and then again about the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it is said that the Republic -- the Government of the Republic of Croatia would advocate the independence and sovereignty of three equal peoples within the borders recognised by the international community. So this is just a repetition ad infinitum of the same positions. Each and every month, all the levels of government in Croatia, urbi et orbi, to the United Nations, the CSCE, the European Community, kept repeating and kept saying the same thing; Bosnia and Herzegovina is a sovereign, independent state. But of course what they supported was an agreement between the three constituent peoples, equal peoples, but of course it couldn't be done because Serbs had a vast supremacy in weapons, and that lasted until 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this topic, I am trying to find something logical. I don't wish to speculate. If you look at page 500, on page 20 of the translated text, on the 2nd of April, 1992, Mr. Greguric says as follows: "The war seems to be spreading to Bosnia and Herzegovina." And I read what is written here. If it's true, I shall bear this in mind. I cannot discard this. He says diplomacy and representatives of the Republic of Croatia pledged for the recognition of ABiH in all conferences, so he claims that the Croatian government is pledging for the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. First of all, is it -- does it make sense to tell the entire world that the republic needs to be recognised, when there are ideas about its annexation? So I'm trying to make sense of this. In April 1992, as far as you were concerned, the Croatian government, let me remind you that you were vice-minister at some point in time, that the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina was something which was pledged by you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everywhere, at every forum, at every time, with the European Community, the CSCE, at every -- well, Your Honours, I would love the whole of this book to be translated so that all of those -- well, those would be piles of materials. And just a few days afterwards, Croatia recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina. Well, of course, there's no logic, there's no logic, Your Honours, in somebody thinking that all this is being done and at the same time we wanted to cheat, to trick the European Community, the CSCE, the USA. And this government, and Franjo Tudjman, and the parliament, and Praljak, are so "stupid," in inverted commas, that they're saying one thing to the whole world and then they manage to sell something else underhand. Do I look like a moron? Look at me. And what about Franjo Tudjman and all the rest? It really makes no sense. There's no logic in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, we saw a piece of evidence which was admitted; i.e., the minutes of a meeting you held with French diplomats and high-ranking military in Zagreb. Looking at the names of the participants, you had the highest-ranking diplomats, French diplomats. During this meeting which you attended, was the fact that Croatia had a hidden agenda vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were [as interpreted], and it is crystal clear, Your Honours. I told the French general, in no uncertain terms, and to the French delegation at that meeting and at every other meeting, our interest in Bosnia and Herzegovina was some kind of a self-government, for crying out loud, but I claim now, and this is what I knew before, Serbs and Muslims, who lost because they were unprepared, and I'm not blaming somebody because they were unprepared for the war, but it is a fact that they were unprepared for the war, they didn't want to see what any blind person could see, that Serbs had been preparing for years, for centuries, for the war and lost a lot of territory. And now that party, the BH Army, is trying to take territory from us, and that -- that's what happened. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I knew that, and that's what I said there. I said -- and that is -- I was working on achieving peace up until May or June, the 30th of April, but you can work on achieving peace, but please look at this document at page 500. Ajanovic said in public, in April, that he and -- and he is a high-ranking official in the Democratic Action Party, he says, he, Ajanovic, does not believe that the army is an occupying force. Yes, Ajanovic said that the Yugoslav People's Army was an occupying force, and now Mr. Izetbegovic says, I don't think that it is an occupying force. If Ajanovic did indeed say that, he went beyond his powers, because he did not present the position of the Democratic Action Party. Well, you can hardly find something worse because on the 2nd of April, Mr. Izetbegovic is claiming that the army in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA, was not an occupying army. It's been shelling us, there are casualties galore, in Mostar and elsewhere, and now you're all supposed to pursue a policy, you're supposed to be engaged in politics, and you're asking yourselves what to do. Please, put yourself in a position where you face this kind of a political view. You are being killed, your children, your families, your people, the Muslims and everything, and now Ajanovic, who is the kind of person that he is, he says, well, they're an occupier, and Izetbegovic says, Well, no, no, they're not supposed to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's been said many times, but perhaps General Praljak can be reminded that if he wishes what he says to be recorded, he really must speak slowly. It's very difficult to follow at the express pace that he is intent on delivering his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You speak very fast, Mr. Praljak, and when interpreters do not express what you say, you can see the sign in the transcript. I happen to speak fast too at times, my apologies for that, but do endeavour to slow down. And thank you, Mr. Khan, for saying that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One word was missed because of the speed, and it's very important for the transcript. That's at page 84, line 15, right at the very beginning the general said, "We were asked," and in the transcript it reads -- the word "asked" is not there. So it should read, "We were asked."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would, of course, like to finish. So on the 2nd of April, 1992, a high-ranking official, the spokesperson for the Party of Democratic Action, Irfan Ajanovic, said that the Yugoslav People's Army was an occupying force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the president of that same party and the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, publicly denied Ajanovic's statement, saying, quote, "I don't think that the army is an occupying force." And if Ajanovic did indeed say that, he went beyond his authority, because this is not the position of the Party of Democratic Action. Would you, all of you here in this courtroom, as individuals and as a people, let yourself be guided by this policy at the time when the Yugoslav People's Army is killing you, has been killing you for months throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, as far as I know, Mostar, and all other towns were bombarded from the air and shelled? We've seen evidence of that. This is incomprehensible, and you cannot force any people, any nation, to accept that, to accept the army that has been killing them, and to understand what Mr. Izetbegovic means when he says, No, no, no, that's not true, that's not an occupying force. So I don't have anything else to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let us finish with the book.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have the last portion to go through.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the 17th. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The last one is the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the current situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yes, the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's page 33 in the translation; e-court 3D41-0408, 3D41-1398, that's the Croatian version. 3D41-1398, that's Croatian, 1398, and page 33 in the English translation. General, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since we should really finish this, there's nothing I can add to this. I would just kindly ask you to read this, all of you. Again, the government, after this resolution, 758, is urging the institutions and organisations, under threat of military force, to stop the aggression against Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and says, Regardless of the fact that you impose sanctions, this has been to no avail. The Government of the Republic of Croatia has several times over the past year insisted that weapons of the JNA should be placed under international control, and goes on to say that there was an ultimatum to Croatia, to allow the pullout of the heavy weapons owned by the JNA from the blockaded barracks to Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the government says, We've been telling you that this would lead to an attack on Bosnia and Herzegovina. Well, everybody knew that. And in spite of all that, the moderators of this war, the international moderators, blind as bats, I don't know why, demanded that the weapons should be pulled out from Croatia into Bosnia and Herzegovina, the JNA weapons. And then it goes on to say how many refugees were taken in in the course of two months and how, again from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Dubrovnik, Slavonski Brod are being attacked and so on, and there's nothing we can add to this. I'm really sorry, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. I'm driven by the desire to finish this. Well, I have nothing more to add to this. I'm ready to answer your questions. And we will submit the whole book to Their Honours, and if anyone wants to check whether my selection was proper, please go ahead. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Praljak, just a question of terminology or vocabulary. I do attach great importance to terminology. This book you are showing us is very interesting, and on this page related to the 8th of June, the author speaks of -- you were a general. Is this the kind of terminology you use to describe the weaponry of armed forces? This kind of language, doesn't it show that the author is biased in the way he sets out the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't see it. I can't really find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 582. The date is the 8th of June: "The current situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In paragraph 3, reference is made to refugees, and there were 270.000 coming in from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the space of two months, and the government says that the international community was not helping enough and that Croatia just couldn't solve the problem itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's the previous paragraph, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I don't know that Judge Mindua's question actually -- it may not have been translated fully, because I know that the question that Judge Mindua asked is not fully in the English transcript, so it's possible that it didn't make it to the witness as well, particularly the reference to the instruments of killing. I don't believe that that is in the English transcript, and so that may be the cause of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll put the question again to the witness. Witness, there is a paragraph that shows the situation, the current situation, as it is said, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the date being the 8th of June. Take the third paragraph. In this paragraph, the author uses some rather harsh words, "killing instruments of the former JNA," he says. Well, I suppose that armed forces have weapons, and, as such, in and of themselves, weapons are weapons. They cannot be qualified as he does here, so my question is whether this type of terminology is not a sign that the author has some rather biased, one-sided views of the issue. What do you think of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua, that's not what it says there, the interpretation that I got. This isn't the position of an author. It is the conclusion of a government, and it says there -- it was sent to the international community, and it says that there was no longer any justification for procrastination on the part of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene at this point? I apologise, but may I be of assistance. I think we'll get through this quicker. If you look at the second paragraph, he says: "The Government of the Republic of Croatia has insisted several times during the past year that the heavy weapons, heavy armament, and other lethal weapons of the former JNA be placed under international control." Judge Mindua says -- is asking whether this term --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Well, interpreter's note, killing instruments, lethal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say that the translation there is wrong in the text. When Defence counsel Senka, our interpreters here said "lethal weapons," and I think that is correct. The correct interpretation is "lethal weapons," whereas the translation that Judge Mindua is reading says "killing instruments," "killing weapons," and that's where the misunderstanding arose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua, "ubojita sredstva", meaning "lethal weapons" means all weapons that kill, so quite simply it's a military term for "military arsenal." "Lethal weapons" is the correct term for "ubojita sredstvo," or "ubojita sredstva" in the plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what is curious to me, because we know that weapons are means of destruction, but is this an honourable way of qualifying the weaponry of an armed force? Does this not show the author's bias regarding the intentions and the behaviour of a given army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be better if you read in your own language that part of the text so that it be interpreted properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honours, but I would have written "ubojita sredstva," the French Army, American Army, meaning "lethal weapons," that's the phrase, "lethal weapons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Government of the Republic of Croatia has insisted several times during the past year that heavy weapons or heavy armament and other lethal weapons of the former JNA be placed under international control," full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's much better in B/C/S than it is in English, because the expression used in English is harsher, so it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, they're ordinary weapons which we refer to as lethal weapons, the lethal weapons of the 6th Fleet or whatever other army you want to use. The term used is "lethal weapons." There's no connotation, political or otherwise. That's what these resources are called, "lethal weapons." A rifle is a lethal weapon, a pistol is a lethal weapon, heavy weapons are lethal weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, isn't it simply a matter of bad drafting, because I cannot see a difference between "armament" and "lethal weapons." It's pleonastic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say, since I happened to deal with disarmament for a number of years with the United Nations, that "lethal weapons" is not -- cannot be equated to "armaments," as such, because there are certain weapons, which -- like chemical weapons, et cetera, which are considered as lethal weapons, and they are not the same like, I don't know, the kind of guns and any other, so to say, rather well-known weapons from history. So, therefore, I think that there could be a distinction made between the two. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, as to the head of the government at the time, didn't he refer to other weaponry than tanks, or rifles, or guns? Did he think of other types of weapons or destruction weapons, like bacteriological or chemical weapons? Didn't he rather have that sort of weaponry in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Your Honours, I can say with a great degree of certainty here that the interpretation of His Honour Judge Trechsel is correct. It is a lot of meaning in one word, but it's just a phrase. You can just say "weapons," but then you add "lethal weapons." It's really nonsensical, but it's the customary phrase used, "lethal weapons." That's the usual term, those two words together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be a little more complex than this, Mr. Praljak. Do not forget that the US intervention in Iraq was connected to the presence of weapons of mass destruction, so it might be a little more complicated. Let's us move on, Ms. Pinter. We have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stay by -- stand by what I said. I know how this was used in political speech. All he means here is that those weapons --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Whose weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons of the Yugoslav People's Army. I don't have to say it 100 times. The Yugoslav People's Army had the weapons. And Croatia asked for something very simple; that the international community come in and then take these weapons and seal them off in the barracks of the Republic of Croatia and place them under its control; that they have soldiers there, whereas the recruits and other soldiers could go home, or wherever they wanted to go. The Serbs did not want to agree to this, or, rather, the JNA, and the international community then gave way, they gave in, and gave Croatia an ultimatum; A, not to attack the barracks and, B, that it wouldn't seal off the barracks with the weapons and leave them where they were, but they asked that it be allowed to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that had catastrophic consequences. And I'm not sure -- I wasn't sure then or -- I didn't understand then, I don't understand now, who were these people who asked that of us, and what were they thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. We've finished with the book.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You mentioned several times -- well, you said today that in November you were in Sunja. How -- when did you get to Sunja, and what can you tell Their Honours about your stay in Sunja? What was the situation there that you found when you arrived, and what year was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a volunteer, an infantryman, I arrived in Sunja on the 3rd of September, 1991. I left Sunja at around the 10th of December -- or, rather, the 10th or 12th of March, 1992. I have a sketch of the position there. It's on the right bank of the Sava River. We were at a position there, at the bridge head. May we have that on the ELMO, please, on the overhead projector? Thank you. We were there for seven or eight days, because of my involvement there. And the gentleman who came was to go back.
