They appointed me commander, anyway, so I was the commander over there for a space of six months and ten days, roughly. It is impossible, in the short time at my disposal, to tell you about Sunja, so let me just say a few sentences, let me put it in a nutshell. Apart from a company from the 2nd Guards Brigade over there, all the rest were villagers, farmers. These are the positions, looking at this sketch [indicates]. This is the Sava River in the background here [indicates]. The length of our front-line was about 30 kilometres. As the crow flies, that would be 20 kilometres, and these are the various villages around Sunja [indicates], and this in the middle is Sunja itself, Sunja proper [indicates]. Sunja was inhabited by Croats and Serbs, and according to the customary scenario what happened was that a vast majority of Serbs from Sunja left and the next day there would be an attack against the Croats who were there and the remaining Serbs. Now, the friends and relatives and the relationships that were set up between Croats and Serbs didn't inform their friends that they were going to flee from Sunja during the night and that they would be attacked the next day, and this destroyed the social structure of a place like Sunja. When you find yourself faced with a situation of that kind, where you have a few dozen units and so on, whatever laws exist in any state, as far as I know, to the best of my knowledge, laws are valid for as long as the citizens of that particular state believe in those laws. This is something I read, written by a US Supreme Court judge at one time with respect to the functioning of American courts; it wasn't because the laws were good, but because the people believed in those laws. So I have to crystallise the situation, in the sense of accepting legality and the laws, you -- whereas you have a totally destroyed social and moral and psychological situation, you have to impose -- you have to put in great effort, impose a system of sanctions. You have to talk to people, punish them, forgive them. You have to deal with this situation of complete social disintegration. Now, how I did this would take me days to tell you, but in the space of one month I did manage to introduce a great deal of law and order, both in military terms and in civilian terms. I was both a commander and I married people in churches, I distributed food, and all the Serbs and Croats there received food. They had what they needed. Not a single house was touched. I even had telephone communications with the opposite side. In a Serb house, for example, I let out the water from the radiators to prevent the house from flooding, because he'd asked me to do this before the winter so that the pipes wouldn't burst. Anyway, Your Honours, I have witness statements from all levels of witnesses, Dusko Ljustina, and Branko Vuksic and Enes Sadikovic, they all provided me with statements, Ranko Radovic, too, and Armin Bajramovic, and Benkovic, and Ivica Cuk, another one, Ivica Istuk, and E-i-d, a Palestinian -- Eid, a Palestinian who was a doctor down there. So is this not an example of how you create an organised structure, how a commander is supposed to behave. And I hope you'll call me once again, once you read all this, for a testimony of one to two hours for me to give you -- supply you with additional answers, to give you more answers as to how I behaved from the beginning of the war to the end, what my conduct was. The front was the best organised in Croatia, from food to other things, and witnesses were Serbs and Croats and Muslims, all of them who fought over there. And when I tell you that I had two Serbs as signalsmen, whose friends and families were on the other side, then what I'm saying is that I trusted them. I had confidence in people, beyond any ethnic considerations. And I also claim that no commander from any Western country would have acted like that because it was too risky. But I believed those two brothers, I trusted them, and that's all I have to say. So you can read it for yourselves, you can read the statements these men gave in a court of law. And even if you have the smallest criticism, then make your decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, before we conclude, we have 3D03567. I would like to ask the Court Deputy to hand this document to the Judges. This is what it looks like [indicates]. It's entitled "Hemingway." General, could you please tell us who Miro Medjimorec is? Could you tell us who Hemingway is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be quick, please, because it's already 7.00. So in two words, tell us who this is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it's not "Medjimurec," it's "Medjimorec." He's one of the best directors in the former Yugoslavia. He worked in theatre. He is my close friend, he has been a close friend of mine since the 1970s. And as a volunteer, he came to Sunja a few days after I did, together with a great theatre actor, stage actor, Sven Lasta. We did this job together. He wrote a book about Hemingway. Well, because of my beard and because of my style, they called me "Hemingway." Throughout the war in Sunja, they used this nickname for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the facts that he's describing in this part, does this correspond to what you really experienced there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the facts from all the statements correspond to the actual situation in Sunja, developments there, and I would really urge the Judges and the Prosecution to read it and then to ask any additional questions they might have to clarify matters, how one can achieve structure and organisation in an area, what one should do. And could we please have the IC number for this?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say that this is under 3D02994 in e-court, and you can see the title page of the book, and who published the book, and all the relevant details for the book to be even discussed. And as regards the defence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we missed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we need to get an IC number for the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An IC number for the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the map shall be given Exhibit IC1028. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I needed some 15 minutes to speak about the Mujahedin, but we'll have to skip that. I had some details from three books, but unfortunately it makes no sense for me to take up any more of your time. But let me just note that those three books, two were published by the Muslims -- well, perhaps you should ask me about the Mujahedin presence, how -- and about its destructive influence on the relationship between Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But at any rate, this completes my testimony in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already spoken a lot about the Mujahedin. Since we have a pending motion filed by Mr. Prlic, it is not ruled out that you might be given these extra 15 minutes, but we shall discuss this among Judges. I have no problem with that at all, personally. On Monday, next Monday, we can speak about the Mujahedin, and then I can start with my questions, but we'll discuss this to see whether my fellow Judges agreed with that or not. For everybody's information, let me tell you that you have used 40 hours and 3 minutes, so the Prosecution will have 40 hours for their cross-examination and the other Defence teams will have 20 hours. Everybody will receive the list of the documents I intend to use. You'll receive this by e-mail, and I do urge you to read the e-mail carefully to make sure that I've sent the list, to avoid any problem next Monday during the hearing. This being said, I wish you all a good evening, and we shall reconvene next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
